'''''Trachycarpus fortunei''''', also known as the '''Chusan palm''',<ref name=iucn/><ref name="bean4">Bean, W. J. (1980). ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles'', 8th ed., vol. 4. John Murray. {{ISBN|0-7195-2428-8}}.</ref><ref name="rhs">{{cite web |title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Trachycarpus fortunei'' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/18291/Trachycarpus-fortunei/Details |access-date=5 March 2021 |publisher=RHS}}</ref> '''Chinese windmill palm''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRFO3|taxon=Trachycarpus fortunei|access-date=14 December 2015}}</ref>  '''hemp palm''',<ref name=usda/> or simply '''windmill palm''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trachycarpus fortunei (Chinese Fan Palm, Chinese Windmill Palm, Chusan Palm, Fortune's Palm, Windmill Palm). North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/trachycarpus-fortunei/ |access-date=24 January 2025 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] [[evergreen]] palm tree in the [[family (botany)|family]] [[Arecaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to parts of China, Japan, Myanmar and India.

==Description==
Growing to {{convert|12-20|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall, ''Trachycarpus fortunei'' is a single-stemmed [[fan palm]]. The trunk is up to {{convert|15-30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} diameter, with a very rough texture with the persistent leaf bases clasping the stem as layers of coarse dark grey-brown fibrous material. The [[leaf|leaves]] have long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s which are bare except for two rows of small spines, terminating in a rounded fan of numerous leaflets. Each leaf is {{convert|140|–|190|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} long, with the petiole {{convert|60|–|100|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} long, and the leaflets up to {{convert|90|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} long. It is a somewhat variable plant, especially as regards its general appearance; and some specimens are to be seen with leaf segments having straight and others having drooping tips.<ref name="Huxley-Griffiths-1992">{{cite book |last1=Huxley |first1=Anthony |last2=Griffiths |first2=Mark |title=Dictionary of Gardening |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] ([[Macmillan Press]]) |publication-place=London |date=1992 |isbn=978-0-333-47494-5 |oclc=25202760}} 3: 443–448, 4: 491.</ref>
[[File:Fleurs Trachycarpus fortunei.jpg|thumb|Trachycarpus fortunei flowers]]
The flowers are yellow (male) and greenish (female), about {{convert|2-4|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} across, borne in large branched panicles up to {{convert|1|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} long in spring; it is [[dioecy|dioecious]], with male and female flowers produced on separate trees. The fruit is a yellow to blue-black, reniform (kidney-shaped) [[drupe]] {{convert|10-12|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long, ripening in mid-autumn.<ref name=foc/><ref name=rhs/>
[[File:Palmier chanvre MHNT.jpg|thumb|''Trachycarpus fortunei'' - Stipe [[MHNT]]]]

==Distribution and habitat==
This plant has been cultivated in China and Japan for thousands of years. This makes tracking its natural range difficult. It is believed to originate in central China ([[Hubei]] southwards), southern Japan ([[Kyushu]]), south to northern Myanmar and [[northern India]], growing at altitudes of {{convert|100|-|2400|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}.<ref name=usda/><ref name=foc>{{cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Flora of China (series)|Flora of China]] |entry-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200027121 |entry=Trachycarpus fortunei |volume=23 |page=145}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=National Institute for Environmental Studies – ''Trachycarpus fortunei'' |url=https://www.nies.go.jp/biodiversity/invasive/DB/detail/80780e.html |access-date=7 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=kew>WCSP, World Checklist of Selected Plant Families: [http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/synonomy.do?name_id=207159 ''Trachycarpus fortunei'']</ref>

''Trachycarpus fortunei'' is one of the [[hardy palms|hardiest palms]]. It tolerates cool, moist summers as well as cold winters, as it grows at much higher altitudes than other species, up to {{convert|2400|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} in the mountains of southern China.<ref name=foc/> However, it is not the northernmost naturally occurring palm in the world, as European fan palm (''[[Chamaerops humilis]]'') grows farther north in the Mediterranean.<ref name=rhs/>

==Uses==
''Trachycarpus fortunei'' has been cultivated in China and Japan for thousands of years, for its coarse but very strong leaf sheath fibre, used for making rope, sacks, and other coarse cloth where great strength is important. The extent of this cultivation means that the exact natural range of the species is uncertain.<ref name=foc/><ref name=rhs/>

===Cultivation===
''Trachycarpus fortunei'' is cultivated as a trunking palm in gardens and parks throughout the world in warm temperate and subtropical climates. Its tolerance of cool summers and cold winters makes it valued by palm enthusiasts, landscape designers and gardeners. It is grown successfully in cool climates such as the UK, Ireland, France, Belgium, The Netherlands, coastal Poland as well as southern and western Germany. In the UK it has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="rhs"/><ref>{{cite web |date=July 2017 |title=AGM Plants – Ornamental |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |access-date=24 December 2018 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |page=103}}</ref>

The tallest reported in cultivation is {{cvt|16.1|m}} tall, in a park at [[Uhart-Mixe]], in Pyrénées-Atlantiques, France.<ref>{{cite web |last1=DBZT |title=Chusan Palm in the park of Château, Uhart-Mixe, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, France |url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/fra/pyreneesatlantiques/uhartmixe/16540_chteau/38811/ |website=Monumental Trees |access-date=8 February 2026}}</ref>

Due to its widespread use as an ornamental plant, the palm has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in southern regions of Switzerland, and has become an invasive species of concern.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Tonelotto M, Fehr V, Conedera M, etal |title=Iconic but Invasive: The Public Perception of the Chinese Windmill Palm (''Trachycarpus fortunei'') in Switzerland |journal=Environmental Management |date=2022 |volume=70 |issue=4 |pages=618–632 |doi=10.1007/s00267-022-01646-3 |pmid=35474487 |pmc=9439986 |bibcode=2022EnMan..70..618T |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In North America, mature specimens can be found growing in the coastal areas of the [[Pacific Northwest]], the [[Upland South|Upper South]], and [[Mid-Atlantic states]]. They can found growing along the West Coast from California north to coastal southwestern British Columbia, and along the East Coast from [[North Florida|northern Florida]] to coastal Connecticut. Lower tolerance limits of {{convert|-15|to|-20|C|F}} are commonly cited for mature plants.<ref name="bean4"/> Young{{specify}} plants are less hardy, and can be damaged by only {{convert|-8|C|F}}. Lowest cold tolerance of well documented specimens include in [[Plovdiv, Bulgaria]], which has survived a low temperature of -27.5 °C.<ref name="c729">{{cite web |last=Donov |first=Kiril |title=Trachycarpus 'Plovdiv' |website=The Polar Palms of Bulgaria |date=6 January 1993 |url=http://www.polarpalm.net/en/plov.html |language=bg |access-date=1 November 2024}}</ref><ref name="Petrova-Vladimirov-2018">{{cite journal |first1=Ana |last1=Petrova |first2=Vladimir |last2=Vladimirov |title=Recent progress in floristic and taxonomic studies in Bulgaria |date=15 February 2018 |doi=10.5281/zenodo.1173552 |journal=[[Botanica Serbica]] |volume=42 |pages=35–69 |issue=1}}</ref><ref name="Sokolov-et-al-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Sokolov |first1=Rosen S. |last2=Shalamanov |first2=Stanimir |last3=Marinov |first3=Vladimir |title=Species composition and self-reproduction ability of trees and shrubs in Plovdiv Municipality |journal=[[Phytologia Balcanica]] |s2cid=89760908 |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=193–203}}</ref> 

The cultivar group [[Trachycarpus fortunei 'Wagnerianus'|''Trachycarpus fortunei'' 'Wagnerianus']] is a small-leafed semi-dwarf variant of the species selected in cultivation in China and Japan. It differs in rarely growing to more than {{convert|5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall, with leaflets less than {{cvt|45|cm|ftin}} long; the short stature and small leaves give it greater tolerance of wind exposure.<ref name=rhs/> It has often been treated as a separate species ''T. wagnerianus'' in popular works, but is now included within ''T. fortunei''.<ref name=kew/><ref name=foc/><ref name=usda/>

=== Cuisine ===
The young flower buds are cooked and eaten in a variety of ways.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stuart |first=G. A. |title=Chinese materia medica Pt. 1 Vegetable kingdom |date=1977 |publisher=Southern Materials Center |isbn=0879684690 |pages=102}}</ref>

==Nomenclature==
The species was brought from Japan (specifically the trading post of [[Dejima]]) to Europe by the German physician [[Philipp Franz von Siebold]] in 1830. The common name refers to Chusan Island (now [[Zhoushan Island]]), where [[Robert Fortune]] first saw cultivated specimens. In 1849, Fortune smuggled plants from China to the Kew Horticultural Gardens and the Royal garden of [[Albert, Prince Consort|Prince Albert]] of the United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Windmill Palm Trees – Tropical Accent Plants – Cold Hardy for Northern United States and Canadian Gardens |url=https://www.tytyga.com/Windmill-Palm-Trees-Tropical-Accent-Plants-Cold-Hardy-for-Northern-United-States-and-Canadian-Gardens-a/444.htm |access-date=6 March 2024 |website=www.tytyga.com}}</ref> It was later named ''Trachycarpus fortunei'', after him. It was first described by Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius in 1850 in his ''Historia Naturalis Palmarum'' but under the illegitimate name of ''Chamaerops excelsa''.

The names ''Chamaerops excelsus'' and ''Trachycarpus excelsus'' have occasionally been misapplied to ''Trachycarpus fortunei''; these are correctly synonyms of ''[[Rhapis excelsa]]'', with the confusion arising due to a misunderstanding of Japanese vernacular names.<ref name=bean4/>
